title: Fiber and scheduling concepts
description: Explore React's Fiber architecture and how its scheduler assigns priorities to work so the UI stays responsive during large updates.

data.text: Before React 16, the renderer used a recursive algorithm that blocked the main thread until the entire tree was finished. **Fiber** replaced that design with a linked-list unit of work that can be paused, split, and resumed. The **scheduler** then decides which fibers to process next based on priority.

Every React element has a corresponding Fiber node. A Fiber stores the component type, state, effects, and pointers to its parent, child, and sibling. This linked-list structure replaces deep recursion and lets React walk the tree iteratively.

items: Links to parent, first child, and next sibling
Stores pending state, effects, and work-in-progress data
Two versions exist: current and work-in-progress

data.text: React assigns each update a priority. Higher-priority work — like a button click — jumps ahead of lower-priority work — like an offscreen analytics render. This prevents urgent interactions from feeling laggy.

rows: Runs only when browser is free

data.text: When an update is scheduled, React does not execute it immediately. Instead, it asks the browser for an idle callback, then walks the Fiber tree and processes units of work one at a time. If the browser needs to handle user input, React pauses, yields, and resumes later.

data.caption: How React's scheduler walks Fiber nodes and yields to the browser.

data.title: Transitions show scheduling in action
data.content: useTransition marks an update as non-urgent so the scheduler can interleave it with user input.

data.title: Think in units of work
data.text: A single setState may spawn many Fiber units. The scheduler processes them one by one, so a component tree with thousands of nodes still yields to the browser between batches.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Fiber replaces recursive rendering with an iterative linked list
The scheduler assigns priorities so urgent work runs first
Low-priority updates can be interrupted and resumed
useTransition is the user-facing API for scheduling non-urgent work
data.takeaway: If a large list update freezes typing, wrap the heavy work in a transition so the scheduler can keep the input responsive.
